answer.short: Both have circumference $18\pi\text{ m}$ and diameter $18\text{ m}$, so they are the same size.
answer.worked:
Circle 1:
$$\begin{align*}C_1&=2\pi r\\C_1&=2\times\pi\times9\\C_1&=18\pi\text{ m}\end{align*}$$
Circle 2:
$$\begin{align*}C_2&=\pi d\\C_2&=\pi\times18\\C_2&=18\pi\text{ m}\end{align*}$$
A radius of $9\text{ m}$ gives a diameter of $18\text{ m}$. Both circles therefore have the same diameter and circumference.

content.prompt:
Which sushi roll has the larger circumference?
One with a radius 20 mm or one with a diameter 4.5 cm? Justify your answer. Give calculated circumferences to 2 decimal places.

answer.short: The roll with diameter $4.5\text{ cm}$: $141.37\text{ mm}$ compared with $125.66\text{ mm}$.
answer.worked:
For the roll with radius $20\text{ mm}$:
$$\begin{align*}C_1&=2\pi r\\C_1&=2\times\pi\times20\\C_1&\approx125.66\text{ mm}\end{align*}$$
For the roll with diameter $4.5\text{ cm}$:
$$\begin{align*}d&=45\text{ mm}\\C_2&=\pi d\\C_2&=\pi\times45\\C_2&\approx141.37\text{ mm}\end{align*}$$
Since $141.37>125.66$, the roll with diameter $4.5\text{ cm}$ has the larger circumference.

content.prompt:
Darling Harbour is planning to install a new Ferris wheel. The wheel has a diameter of 80 m.
The pods can carry 10 passengers each but need to be spaced out by at least 10 m around the circumference of the Ferris wheel.
What is the maximum number of passengers that can be on the Ferris wheel at one time?

answer.short: 250 passengers (25 pods; round down to satisfy the minimum spacing).
answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}C &= \pi\times80=80\pi\text{ m}\\\text{Number of pods} &\leq \frac{80\pi}{10}=8\pi\\8\pi &\approx 25.13\end{align*}$$
The maximum whole number of pods is 25, since the spacing must be at least 10 m.
$$\begin{align*}\text{Maximum passengers} &= 25\times10\\\text{Maximum passengers} &= 250\end{align*}$$

answer.worked:
The thread is the radius of the circular path.
$$\begin{align*}
r &= \frac{80}{100}=0.8\text{ m}\\
\text{Revolutions} &= \frac{4230}{360}=11.75\\
\text{Distance} &= 11.75\times 2\pi r\\
\text{Distance} &= 11.75\times 2\pi\times 0.8\\
\text{Distance} &= 18.8\pi\text{ m}\\
\text{Distance} &\approx 59.06\text{ m}
\end{align*}$$

answer.worked:
Halving the circumference gives only the curved edge. The perimeter also includes the $7\text{ cm}$ diameter.
$$\begin{aligned}P&=\frac12\pi d+d\\P&=\frac12\pi(7)+7\\P&=\frac{7\pi}{2}+7\text{ cm}\\P&\approx18\text{ cm}\quad\text{(nearest whole centimetre)}\end{aligned}$$

inlines.text: Sean’s frisbee has a radius of 12 cm.
He cuts it into sectors of
and turns both into smaller frisbees.
The curved arc of each sector becomes the circumference of its new frisbee.

spec.sourceRegion: Question 8, left figure beneath the stem
spec.description: Separated major and minor sectors from the original frisbee, with central angles and the original radius retained.
spec.mathematics: Both sectors have radius 12 cm. Their central angles are 202.5° and 157.5°, summing to 360°. Matching radial edges are separated by a visible gap.
spec.answerVisibility: All geometry and labels are permanent student givens.

spec.sourceRegion: Question 8, smaller circle to the right of the separated sectors
spec.description: The new frisbee made from the larger sector: an unshaded complete circle with a centre dot and a horizontal radius labelled r cm.
spec.mathematics: The circumference of this new circle equals the arc length of the original 202.5° sector. Its radius is unknown.
spec.answerVisibility: The radius label r cm is a permanent unknown, with no numerical answer shown.

answer.short: $6.75\text{ cm}$. The larger sector’s arc becomes the new frisbee’s circumference.
answer.worked:
The $202.5^\circ$ sector has the longer arc, so it makes the bigger frisbee. Let its arc length be $\ell$.
$$\begin{align*}\ell &= \frac{\theta}{360}\times2\pi R\\\ell &= \frac{202.5}{360}\times2\pi(12)\\\ell &= \frac{27\pi}{2}\text{ cm}\end{align*}$$
This arc becomes the circumference of the new frisbee.
$$\begin{align*}C &= 2\pi r\\\frac{27\pi}{2} &= 2\pi r\\\frac{27\pi/2}{2\pi} &= r\\r &= \frac{27}{4}\\r &= 6.75\text{ cm}\end{align*}$$

questionDiagrams.retentionReason: Complex illustrative raster of a globe with irregular continents, curved belt, buckle, overlap and photographic shading. It contains no mathematical labels or dimensions; native reconstruction would change the supplied illustration.

answer.short: $0.16\text{ m}$; half the difference of the diameters.
answer.worked:

inlines.text: Flo uses a tape measure to find the circumference of a tree trunk.
She finds the circumference is 150 cm. She divided by 3 to estimate the diameter of the trunk.

answer.short: Since $C=\pi d$ and $\pi\approx3$, dividing the circumference by 3 estimates the diameter.
answer.worked: The circumference is $\pi$ times the diameter. Using $\pi\approx3$ gives $C\approx3d$, so dividing the circumference by 3 estimates the diameter.

children.label: b
children.prompt: Would the actual diameter be more or less? Why?

answer.short: Less, because $\pi>3$ and dividing by a larger positive number gives a smaller result.
answer.worked: The estimated diameter is $150\div3=50\text{ cm}$. The actual diameter is $150\div\pi$. Since $\pi\approx3.14>3$, the actual diameter is smaller than the estimate.

children.label: c
children.prompt: What should she divide by to estimate the radius?

answer.short: Divide the circumference by 6, or divide the estimated diameter by 2.
answer.worked: Using $\pi\approx3$ in $C=2\pi r$ gives $C\approx6r$. Divide the circumference by 6 to estimate the radius. Equivalently, divide the estimated diameter by 2.

content.prompt:
Peter cuts a sector from a circle so that three eighths of the area remains.
If the circle's radius is 5 cm, what is the perimeter of the shape, to the nearest centimetre?

spec.sourceRegion: Question 6, sector beneath the stem on the left
spec.description: Unshaded sector opening to the right, with two radii meeting at the left vertex and the fraction 3/8 inside.
spec.mathematics: The retained sector is three eighths of a circle, so its arc is three eighths of the circumference. Its central angle is 135 degrees; no angle or radius label is printed in the source figure. User-requested radius label: 5 cm.
spec.answerVisibility: The fraction 3/8 is a permanent given. No perimeter answer appears in the question diagram.

answer.worked:
The remaining arc is $\frac{3}{8}$ of the circumference.
$$\begin{align*}
P &= l+2r\\
P &= \frac{3}{8}\times2\pi(5)+2(5)\\
P &= \frac{15\pi}{4}+10\\
P &\approx 22\text{ cm}

inlines.text: Mr Ding is scrolling Instagram and comes across this post:
“If the Earth were round, then planes wouldn’t fly so far up, as they would waste lots of fuel and money. This proves that the earth must be flat!”
Using mathematical reasoning, justify whether this post is factually correct.
The radius of the Earth is around 21 000 000 feet. Planes usually do fly at 33 000 feet.
Round any percentage increase to 2 decimal places.

spec.description: Unshaded planar circular Earth schematic and four outline aircraft preserving the source's upper and lower routes, altitude guides and exaggerated relative arrangement. The Earth outline represents a circular section without 3D meridians or rear surface curves. The fourfold flight-time text remains a source claim.

originalDiagram.retentionReason: The post combines a photographic globe, aircraft silhouettes, handwritten labels and deliberately misleading flight-path scale. The inspected isolated source asset matches the PDF illustration and preserves the essential 5000 ft, 33,000 ft and fourfold-flight-time claims without inventing geometry.

geometry.surfaceCurves: None; the diagram contains no 3D meridians or rear surface curves.
geometry.contextualPaths: Two flight-route arrows, two altitude guides and four aircraft outlines retain their current coordinates.
geometry.labels: The 5000 ft, 33 000 ft and fourfold-flight-time labels retain their current positions and 10 pt native fonts.

spec.intentionalDeparture: Replace the native globe's solid rear surface curves with a planar circular Earth schematic while preserving the misleading altitude arrangement as source evidence for students to evaluate.

inlines.text: The post is incorrect. The circumference ratio is
At the same speed, the flight would take about
longer. The diagram exaggerates the altitudes relative to the Earth’s radius.

answer.worked:
Consider a plane flying around the Earth at each altitude.

At 5000 feet:
$$\begin{align*}r_{5000}&=21\,000\,000+5000=21\,005\,000\text{ ft}\\C_{5000}&=2\pi r_{5000}\\C_{5000}&=2\pi(21\,005\,000)\\C_{5000}&=42\,010\,000\pi\text{ ft}\end{align*}$$

At 33 000 feet:
$$\begin{align*}r_{33000}&=21\,000\,000+33\,000=21\,033\,000\text{ ft}\\C_{33000}&=2\pi r_{33000}\\C_{33000}&=2\pi(21\,033\,000)\\C_{33000}&=42\,066\,000\pi\text{ ft}\end{align*}$$

Comparing the circumferences:
$$\begin{align*}\frac{C_{33000}}{C_{5000}}&=\frac{42\,066\,000\pi}{42\,010\,000\pi}\\\frac{C_{33000}}{C_{5000}}&=\frac{21\,033}{21\,005}\\\frac{C_{33000}}{C_{5000}}&\approx1.001333016\end{align*}$$

The percentage increase is
$$\begin{align*}\text{increase}&=\frac{42\,066\,000\pi-42\,010\,000\pi}{42\,010\,000\pi}\times100\%\\\text{increase}&=\frac{56\,000}{42\,010\,000}\times100\%\\\text{increase}&\approx0.13\%.\end{align*}$$

At the same speed, the flight would take about $0.13\%$ longer, rather than four times as long. The illustration exaggerates the flight altitudes relative to the Earth’s radius, so the post’s mathematical reasoning is incorrect.

3. Solve

entries.description:
Syllabus Content

MA4-LEN-C-01 applies knowledge of the perimeter of plane shapes and the circumference of circles to solve problems

Solve problems involving the perimeter of various quadrilaterals and simple composite figures
• Solve problems involving the perimeter of plane shapes, including parallelograms, trapeziums, rhombuses and kites
• Solve problems relating to the perimeter of simple composite figures
• Compare methods of solution for finding perimeter and evaluate the efficiency of those methods

Describe the relationships between the features of circles
• Identify and describe the relationship between circle features, including the radius, diameter, arc, chord, sector and segment of a circle, and a tangent to a circle
• Define π as the ratio of the circumference to the diameter of any circle
• Verify that the number π is a constant and develop the formula for the circumference of a circle
• Apply the formula for the circumference of a circle in terms of the diameter d or radius r (circumference of a circle C = πd or = 2πr) to solve related problems to solve related problems
• Establish the arc length formula l = (θ/360) × 2πr where l is the arc length and θ is the angle subtended at the centre by the arc
• Solve problems by finding arc lengths and the perimeter of sectors, giving an exact answer in terms of π or an approximate answer
• Find the perimeter of quadrants, semicircles and simple composite figures consisting of 2 shapes in a variety of contexts, including using digital tools

entries.description:
A metre (m) is the basic metric unit used to measure length.
Door handles are about 1 m off the ground.
All other metric units are related to the metre by powers of 10.
1 kilometre (km) = 1000 metres (m)
1 metre (m) = 100 centimetres (cm)
1 centimetre (cm) = 10 millimetres (mm)
We have different units of length to avoid using very small or very large numbers.

The radius of the Earth is around 21 000 000 feet. Planes usually do fly at 33 000 feet.

entries.expectedAnswer:
Consider a plane flying around the Earth.
At 5000 feet, C = 2π(21 005 000) = 42 010 000π
At 33000 feet: C = 2π(21 033 000) = 42 066 000π
Comparing the two: (42 066 000π)/(42 010 000π) = 1.001333016 …
The increase in distance is only 0.13%, so the flight would not take 4 times as long.
The diagram is misleading, as the Earth is not drawn to the correct scale (planes don’t fly in space).
